title: King Trump's AI Propaganda Machine: 62 Deepfakes, a Fighter Jet Dropping Feces on Protesters, and False Crowd Photos
description_medium: WIRED documented Trump’s use of AI-generated posts and described an October 2025 video showing him as “KING TRUMP,” piloting a fighter jet and dropping a substance on fictionalized No Kings protesters in Times Square. The article traces how synthetic images and video became part of his public online presence. It does not substantiate the 62-post total or all examples in the existing long account.
description_long: In October 2025, President Donald Trump shared an AI-generated video depicting himself in a fighter jet marked “KING TRUMP.” The clip showed the plane dropping a brown substance on fictionalized No Kings demonstrators in Times Square. The video circulated shortly after nationwide No Kings protests and prompted discussion of Trump’s use of synthetic political imagery. WIRED’s reporting describes a broader pattern in which Trump posted AI-generated images and videos on his social accounts, sometimes depicting himself in exaggerated or fantastical scenes and sometimes targeting political opponents. A senior White House official told the publication Trump sometimes saved videos he found amusing and posted them. The episode demonstrates the use of altered or fabricated visuals in political communication, but the video was satire or political messaging rather than documentary footage of an actual attack on protesters. The linked WIRED report supports the “KING TRUMP” clip and the general pattern; it does not verify the title’s count of 62 posts, follower counts, or all the separate claims about Pelosi, Obama, a pope image, medbeds, agency posts, and crowd photographs. Those examples require their own sources and should not be inferred from this one report.
evidence_notes: WIRED supports described clip and general pattern. The 62 count and other individual examples require separate sources; clip depicts fictionalized protesters, not real footage of an event.
corrected_wording: Retain or remove the numeric count and additional examples only with the cited NYT/NBC/source records that substantiate them.

title: TRUMP and MELANIA Memecoins: The Presidential Pump-and-Dump That Made $100M in Fees
description_medium: Trump announced the $TRUMP memecoin on January 17, 2025. Reuters later estimated that the coin’s creators collected roughly $86 million to $100 million in trading fees by January 30, while about 200,000 wallets, mostly small holders, lost money. Reuters could not determine how much of those fees reached Trump personally. Its report does not cover the $MELANIA token, establish a pump-and-dump scheme, or substantiate later financial-disclosure figures.
description_long: Donald Trump announced the $TRUMP cryptocurrency token on Truth Social on January 17, 2025, two days before his second inauguration. Reuters reported that the token’s creators had accumulated an estimated $86 million to $100 million in trading fees by January 30, drawing on analyses by blockchain firms. The outlet also reported that roughly 200,000 wallets, most holding relatively small amounts, had lost money trading the token, while at least 50 large investors made more than $10 million each. Those estimates describe trading activity and wallet outcomes over the period Reuters examined. Reuters could not determine how much of the fees went to Trump personally, so the headline-level fee estimate should not be equated with personal income. The provided Reuters report concerns the $TRUMP token; it does not establish the separate claims about Melania Trump’s coin, insider ownership percentages, an early trader’s alleged advance notice, or disclosures made in 2026. Nor does the report itself prove a “pump-and-dump” scheme, which implies intentional manipulation. A reader-facing account should distinguish the token’s launch, estimated creator fees, and reported distribution of gains and losses from claims about individual beneficiaries or legal wrongdoing.
evidence_notes: Reuters report hosted by Yahoo supports launch, estimated fee range and small-wallet losses; expressly could not establish amount reaching Trump. No Melania token or pump-and-dump evidence in this source.
corrected_wording: Add a $TRUMP-only title or separately source the $MELANIA token and any allegation of manipulation.

title: Cover-Up Certified: Judge Permanently Blocks Release of Mar-a-Lago Classified Documents Report
description_medium: On February 23, 2026, U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon barred the Justice Department from releasing special counsel Jack Smith’s report on the Mar-a-Lago documents prosecution. Cannon said release would be unfair because the case ended without a jury verdict. The order concerned disclosure of the report; it did not decide Trump’s guilt, establish a cover-up, or make the report public.
description_long: On February 23, 2026, U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon permanently barred the Justice Department from publicly releasing special counsel Jack Smith’s report on the classified-documents case against Donald Trump. The prosecution accused Trump of unlawfully retaining classified records after leaving office and storing them at Mar-a-Lago. Cannon had dismissed the criminal case in 2024 after ruling that Smith was unlawfully appointed. In the later disclosure ruling, she reasoned that releasing the report would be unfair because the case never reached a jury and it contained substantial allegations of criminal wrongdoing. That order controls public release of the report; it is not a verdict on the underlying allegations and does not establish that evidence was concealed to protect Trump. Reuters reported the ruling and Cannon’s stated reasoning. The prior account also described detailed contents of Smith’s report, including specific intelligence categories and a damage assessment, but those claims cannot be confirmed from the linked public report because the report remains unreleased. The entry can accurately document the court’s restriction and its stated basis while keeping allegations about the report’s contents and any “cover-up” conclusion separate from what the ruling itself established.
evidence_notes: Reuters coverage supports order and stated basis. The report is not public; detailed claims about contents/damage assessment cannot be verified from linked source. “Cover-up certified” overstates the order.
corrected_wording: Consider title: “Judge Blocks Public Release of Jack Smith’s Mar-a-Lago Report.”

title: DOGE AI Surveillance Program Monitors Federal Employees for Anti-Trump Sentiment
description_medium: Reuters reported in April 2025, citing two people familiar with the matter, that DOGE technologists were using AI to scan communications at at least one federal agency for hostility toward Trump and his agenda. The report raised questions about monitoring within the civil service but did not name the agency, define the tool’s scope, or document disciplinary action against employees. Those limits should remain clear when describing the allegation.
description_long: In April 2025, Reuters reported that Trump administration officials had told some federal employees that Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency team was using artificial intelligence to monitor communications at at least one federal agency. Two people familiar with the matter said the scanning sought expressions of hostility toward President Donald Trump or his agenda. The account described an attempt to detect sentiment in government communications, rather than an identified list of monitored workers or a documented disciplinary program. Reuters did not name the agency involved, explain which communication systems were scanned, specify how many employees were covered, or report that the monitoring resulted in firings or other penalties. The report also described DOGE employees’ own use of Signal and collaborative Google documents, but those details do not by themselves show that the government’s employee-monitoring operation violated a particular law. The episode raised concerns about privacy, political neutrality and the limits of government access to internal messages. Because Reuters relied on unnamed sources and described limited scope, the entry should attribute the allegation to the report and preserve those qualifications rather than state that a nationwide surveillance program monitored all federal workers.
evidence_notes: Reuters based allegation on two sources familiar with matter; at least one agency, no agency named or consequence documented. Keep attribution explicit.
corrected_wording: Title should identify this as a Reuters-reported monitoring effort, not imply a fully documented nationwide program.

title: DOJ Office of Legal Counsel Opinion Rejects ADA/Rehabilitation Act Integration Mandate for State Institutionalization
description_medium: On June 18, 2026, the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel issued an opinion concluding that the ADA and Rehabilitation Act do not impose a state integration mandate for people with mental disabilities or authorize federal agencies to impose one. OLC said its interpretation of Olmstead differed from the common understanding in federal courts. The opinion is an executive-branch legal view, not a new statute or court judgment.
description_long: The Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel released an opinion on June 18, 2026, addressing whether Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act require states to provide treatment for people with mental disabilities in the most integrated setting. OLC concluded that those laws do not impose that integration mandate and do not authorize executive agencies to impose it on states. The opinion also interpreted the Supreme Court’s 1999 decision in Olmstead v. L.C., which had been widely understood as applying integration requirements to public services for people with disabilities. OLC acknowledged that its reading departed from the common understanding of Olmstead in federal courts. The opinion represents the Justice Department’s interpretation of the statutes and the authority of executive agencies; it is not a Supreme Court ruling, an act of Congress, or itself a judgment in a case against a state. Senator Tammy Duckworth, joined by Senators Chuck Schumer and Dick Durbin, introduced a resolution urging DOJ to withdraw the opinion and reaffirm disability-rights protections. The event therefore includes both the legal position announced by OLC and a congressional response. The record date should be corrected upstream to June 18, the date DOJ issued the opinion.
evidence_notes: DOJ opinion dated June 18, 2026; official senator release supports subsequent resolution. Existing record date June22 is incorrect.
corrected_wording: Set event date to June 18, 2026. Preserve that this is an OLC legal interpretation, not a court holding.

title: LGBTQ Asylum Seekers Abandoned: Refugee Cap Slashed 94 Percent, White Afrikaners Prioritized
description_medium: For fiscal year 2026, the Trump administration set a refugee admissions ceiling of 7,500, down from the prior year’s 125,000 ceiling, and said admissions would be primarily allocated to Afrikaners from South Africa. Refugee advocates criticized the reduction and narrow priority. The linked presidential determination establishes the cap and stated allocation; it does not itself quantify how many LGBTQ refugees were excluded or prove the effect on any asylum seeker.
description_long: A presidential determination published in October 2025 set the fiscal year 2026 refugee admissions ceiling at 7,500 people, sharply below the 125,000 ceiling established for the preceding fiscal year. The determination said admissions would be primarily allocated to Afrikaners from South Africa under the administration’s policy. This policy addressed the U.S. refugee admissions program, which processes people outside the country who seek resettlement after fleeing persecution; it is distinct from asylum claims made by people already in the United States. Refugee advocates criticized the low ceiling and the decision to prioritize one group, arguing that the policy would reduce access for people fleeing other forms of persecution and conflict. A subsequent 2026 emergency determination raised the ceiling to 17,500 for Afrikaner admissions, showing that the original 7,500 limit was later modified. The supplied presidential determination supports the initial cap and priority but does not document the number of LGBTQ refugees who lost access, establish that LGBTQ applicants were categorically excluded, or prove the broader consequences described in the older draft. Those claims require program data and an analysis specific to LGBTQ applicants. The entry can describe the policy and its critics’ concerns while distinguishing the refugee cap from asylum proceedings and subsequent amendments.
evidence_notes: Initial determination set 7,500 with Afrikaner priority. May 27 2026 emergency determination raised ceiling to 17,500. Neither source quantifies LGBTQ exclusions; do not assert categorical exclusion or specific harms.
corrected_wording: Narrow title to FY2026 refugee cap and Afrikaner prioritization unless specific LGBTQ impact analysis is added.

title: GoTrump.com Travel Site Shuts Down a Year After Launch
description_medium: TIME lists GoTrump.com among Trump-branded ventures and describes the luxury travel site as powered by Travelocity and lasting about a year. The available report supports the basic launch-and-closure chronology, but it does not provide operating figures, the reason for closure, or evidence that the site was a failed business. Those details would be needed to expand this account without adding unsupported judgments.
description_long: GoTrump.com was a travel website associated with Donald Trump and powered by Travelocity’s booking technology. A TIME retrospective on Trump business ventures says the site lasted about a year. The available account identifies it as a luxury travel service and places it among a list of Trump-branded projects, but the retrieved material does not explain its business model in detail, state how many customers used it, report its revenue or costs, or document the reason it closed. The existing draft describes the short duration as proof that the venture “flared quickly and fizzled” and lacked staying power; that is an editorial judgment rather than an independently established outcome. A fuller history would require contemporaneous reporting about the launch, its commercial performance and the shutdown. The cited TIME page was inaccessible through the available retrieval, so this proposal is limited to the facts visible in the supplied record and its search-index summary. It preserves the supported points—the website’s luxury-travel purpose, Travelocity connection and approximate lifespan—while leaving the cause, scale and financial result unresolved.
evidence_notes: TIME search-index summary supports Travelocity-powered luxury travel site lasting one year; page fetch returned HTTP 406 and no article text. Independent contemporaneous source needed for closure date, performance and reason.
corrected_wording: Replace unsupported evaluative sentence with sourced operating or closure details when a readable account is available.
exact_blocker: The only supplied source was inaccessible (HTTP 406) and its available summary provides no operating figures or reason for closure; no adequate factual basis for the requested expanded history is present.

title: ANWR Opened for Drilling on Inauguration Day
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14153 directing federal agencies to promote oil and gas leasing and permitting in Alaska, including the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. The order instructed Interior to revisit canceled leases and take steps toward additional leasing. It changed federal policy but did not itself establish that drilling began or that leases or permits were issued. The supplied order does not support the claim that an Indigenous sacred-site designation was denied.
description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14153, Unleashing Alaska’s Extraordinary Resource Potential, on January 20, 2025. The order directed the Interior Department to promote oil and gas development in Alaska, including the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, and instructed agencies to review lease cancellations and take steps to restore or expand leasing and permitting. It also directed review of environmental actions taken by the prior administration. The Coastal Plain is a roughly 1.5-million-acre area within the refuge and is important to the Gwich’in people, who refer to it as the Sacred Place Where Life Begins because of its relationship to the Porcupine caribou herd. Those cultural and ecological concerns provide context for why development policy is contested, but anticipated harms should not be presented as effects already caused by this order. An executive directive to resume leasing is also not proof that drilling has begun or that a specific permit was approved. The supplied order establishes the change in federal direction; it does not substantiate the separate claim that the administration denied a pending Indigenous sacred-site designation. That claim requires a decision or agency record.
evidence_notes: EO supports agency directives regarding ANWR leasing and environmental review. It neither proves drilling commenced nor a decision denying a sacred-site designation.
corrected_wording: Change “opened for drilling” to “directed agencies to promote leasing and development” unless implementation evidence is added.

title: The Polish Brigade: Trump Tower Built on Undocumented Labor and Wage Theft
description_medium: The 1991 federal court case concerning workers who demolished the Bonwit Teller building for Trump Tower addressed unpaid pension and welfare contributions. The court found that union trustee John Senyshyn breached his fiduciary duty and that Trump-Equitable knowingly participated in that breach, awarding $325,415.84 in unpaid contributions plus interest and costs. The legal finding concerned employee-benefit contributions; it should be distinguished from wage-theft allegations against contractor Kaszycki.
description_long: The “Polish Brigade” case arose from demolition of the Bonwit Teller building on Fifth Avenue before construction of Trump Tower. Workers employed by Kaszycki & Sons Contractors performed the work; the 1991 federal opinion records that most, if not all, of the contractor’s Polish workers were undocumented, worked off the books, received irregular and incomplete pay, and were not paid in accordance with wage laws. The case itself concerned unpaid pension and welfare-fund contributions owed on their wages. After a 16-day bench trial, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York found that union trustee John Senyshyn breached his fiduciary duty and that Trump-Equitable participated in the breach. It also found evidence of a tacit agreement among Kaszycki, Senyshyn and the Trump defendants to employ the workers and deprive the funds of contributions due on their work. The court awarded $325,415.84 in unpaid contributions, interest and attorney fees. The opinion did not hold that Trump-Equitable was the workers’ employer; it found liability for knowing participation in the fiduciary breach. A separate case had found the contractor violated minimum-wage, overtime and recordkeeping rules. This distinction matters because the court’s findings establish a serious link to the project while identifying the specific legal wrong and the parties responsible.
evidence_notes: Primary opinion documents workers’ off-books conditions; after bench trial found Senyshyn breached fiduciary duty and Trump-Equitable knowingly participated in breach to deprive union funds of contributions; awarded $325,415.84 plus interest and fees. Court expressly did not find Trump defendants to be employers. Separate Donovan case found contractor labor-law violations.
corrected_wording: Clarify in title that the case concerned contractor workers and unpaid benefit contributions; separately source any wage theft or unsafe-condition findings.

title: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts Files for Chapter 11 in 2004
description_medium: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts and subsidiaries filed voluntary Chapter 11 petitions in New Jersey on November 21, 2004, as part of a prearranged restructuring. The company’s SEC filing describes it as the predecessor company and reports the bankruptcy process and emergence. This was a corporate reorganization, not a personal bankruptcy by Donald Trump. The title’s “Fourth Chapter 11” wording is not supported by the cited filing and should be removed.
description_long: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts Inc. and certain subsidiaries filed voluntary petitions for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of New Jersey on November 21, 2004. The company’s subsequent SEC filing describes the petitions as part of a prearranged plan of reorganization and reports the company’s emergence from bankruptcy. The process concerned the corporate casino operator and its subsidiaries, rather than a personal bankruptcy filing by Donald Trump. The filing gave the company an opportunity to restructure debts and continue operating while it negotiated with creditors under court supervision. The company’s public disclosures and bankruptcy records are the appropriate sources for the amount of debt, creditor recoveries, management arrangements and precise restructuring terms. The SEC filing supports the filing date and Chapter 11 status, but not the original title’s description as the “fourth” filing. That ordinal conflates different Trump-associated companies and casino properties, whose filings occurred at different times. A careful account should identify the legal entity and distinguish this corporate proceeding from the later bankruptcy of Trump Entertainment Resorts in 2009 and from earlier bankruptcies involving individual casinos.
evidence_notes: SEC 10-K confirms voluntary Chapter 11 filing Nov 21, 2004. Corporate filing, not personal bankruptcy. ‘Fourth’ is unsupported/conflates entities.
corrected_wording: Correct title to identify Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts and remove the “fourth” ordinal.
